scenes.tts: The first film showed that a population needs survivors that reproduce. American chestnut roots still send up living sprouts. Why has that population not recovered?
scenes.caption: The first film showed that a population needs survivors that reproduce. American chestnut roots still send up living sprouts. Why has that population not recovered?
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's COLOR MAP exactly: living chestnut tissue GREEN; inherited resistance bars BLUE; blight and cankers RED; seeds and offspring YELLOW; dead or nonreproducing tissue GREY. Begin below the same forest floor. A large GREEN root fills the lower half of the frame and sends up one leafy sprout. Above ground, faint GREY canopy-tree silhouettes leave an empty opening. A white question grows in that opening while the sprout sways.
scenes.narration: The first film showed that a population needs survivors that reproduce. American chestnut roots still send up living sprouts. Why has that population not recovered?

scenes.visual: Keep the root glowing and the sprout moving. Fade in the title 'From Sprouts to Seed-Making Trees' across the empty canopy opening, then fade it out. A slow camera rise connects the root to the sprout.

scenes.tts: Keep the same colors. Green marks living chestnut tissue, red marks blight, blue marks inherited resistance, and yellow marks seeds. A green root remains underground. It sends a leafy sprout upward.
scenes.caption: Keep the same colors. Green marks living chestnut tissue, red marks blight, blue marks inherited resistance, and yellow marks seeds. A green root remains underground. It sends a leafy sprout upward.
scenes.visual: As each color is named, pulse that carried object: GREEN root and sprout, a small RED canker icon held offstage, a BLUE resistance bar inside the sprout, and YELLOW seed icons dimmed above. A new green stem extends upward from the root and unfolds two leaves. Keep every object in the same locations for the next scenes.
scenes.narration: Keep the same colors. Green marks living chestnut tissue, red marks blight, blue marks inherited resistance, and yellow marks seeds. A green root remains underground. It sends a leafy sprout upward.

scenes.tts: Red fungus grows into a crack in the bark. A canker widens around the young trunk. The trunk above it fades grey, while the protected root stays green. Soon that root sends up another sprout.
scenes.caption: Red fungus grows into a crack in the bark. A canker widens around the young trunk. The trunk above it fades grey, while the protected root stays green. Soon that root sends up another sprout.
scenes.visual: A small crack opens in the sprout's bark. RED specks enter and become a widening red band labeled 'canker'. The stem and leaves above the band gradually turn GREY and lean away. Keep the root GREEN. After the grey trunk slides aside, send another green sprout upward from a different point on the same root.
scenes.narration: Red fungus grows into a crack in the bark. A canker widens around the young trunk. The trunk above it fades grey, while the protected root stays green. Soon that root sends up another sprout.

scenes.tts: The cycle repeats. The forest contains living chestnut stems, but the sprouts rarely become seed-making canopy trees. Living stems alone do not show that the population is recovering.
scenes.caption: The cycle repeats. The forest contains living chestnut stems, but the sprouts rarely become seed-making canopy trees. Living stems alone do not show that the population is recovering.
scenes.visual: Run a schematic loop around the carried root: green sprout rises, red canker widens, trunk fades grey, new sprout rises. Show a small turning clock with no number. The empty canopy opening remains above. YELLOW seed icons stay dim. Add 'schematic' near the loop.
scenes.narration: The cycle repeats. The forest contains living chestnut stems, but the sprouts rarely become seed-making canopy trees. Living stems alone do not show that the population is recovering.

scenes.tts: Freeze the cycle after a new sprout appears. No yellow seeds are present. If every sprout dies before making seeds, can these sprouts rebuild a lasting population?
scenes.caption: Freeze the cycle after a new sprout appears. No yellow seeds are present. If every sprout dies before making seeds, can these sprouts rebuild a lasting population?
scenes.visual: Stop the loop with one GREEN sprout upright and the root still glowing. Show an empty YELLOW seed tray beside it. Across the top, place the question 'Can sprouts alone rebuild the population?' The red canker waits at the edge of the bark. Root light shimmers gently.
scenes.narration: Freeze the cycle after a new sprout appears. No yellow seeds are present. If every sprout dies before making seeds, can these sprouts rebuild a lasting population?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep the question, living root, sprout, and empty seed tray on screen. Only the root shimmer and a slow leaf movement continue. Do not reveal an answer.

scenes.tts: No. Each green sprout proves that living tissue remains, so the species is not extinct. But if sprouts die before making seeds, no new generation replaces the old roots. In the wild, few sprouts make seeds. Survival requires survivors to reproduce, not merely remain alive.
scenes.caption: No. Each green sprout proves that living tissue remains, so the species is not extinct. But if sprouts die before making seeds, no new generation replaces the old roots. In the wild, few sprouts make seeds. Survival requires survivors to reproduce, not merely remain alive.
scenes.visual: Remove the question. Place a green check beside 'living tissue remains'. Then extend a generation arrow from the old root toward an empty space; it stops because the seed tray is empty. The root slowly dims with no replacement. Build the film's rule above the stopped arrow. Do not show extinction or claim when the last root will die.
scenes.narration: No. Each green sprout proves that living tissue remains, so the species is not extinct. But if sprouts die before making seeds, no new generation replaces the old roots. In the wild, few sprouts make seeds. Survival requires survivors to reproduce, not merely remain alive.

scenes.tts: How might people change that path? Breeders begin with American chestnuts and Chinese chestnuts that resist blight better. They cross the trees. Then they expose the offspring to blight.
scenes.caption: How might people change that path? Breeders begin with American chestnuts and Chinese chestnuts that resist blight better. They cross the trees. Then they expose the offspring to blight.
scenes.visual: Slide the sprout cycle left without removing it. On the right, grow two large tree cartoons labeled 'American chestnut' and 'Chinese chestnut'. Show a shorter BLUE resistance bar in the American example and a taller BLUE bar in the Chinese example, labeled 'examples, not every tree'. A YELLOW cross arrow joins the parents and transforms into a row of seedling cartoons. A RED test canker touches each seedling.
scenes.narration: How might people change that path? Breeders begin with American chestnuts and Chinese chestnuts that resist blight better. They cross the trees. Then they expose the offspring to blight.

scenes.tts: Blue resistance bars differ among the offspring. People choose the most resistant young trees. Then they cross those back to American chestnuts and test again. That is artificial selection. People choose which trees reproduce, instead of letting the environment alone decide.
scenes.caption: Blue resistance bars differ among the offspring. People choose the most resistant young trees. Then they cross those back to American chestnuts and test again. That is artificial selection. People choose which trees reproduce, instead of letting the environment alone decide.
scenes.visual: Make the offspring's BLUE bars rise to different heights. RED cankers widen by different amounts. A human hand icon moves only the better-resisting seedlings into a glowing parent ring. A YELLOW cross arrow joins them to a new American chestnut cartoon, and the arrow carries them into a second row of varied offspring. Label the repeating action 'artificial selection'. Keep the unchosen seedlings visible but neutral, not marked rejected.
scenes.narration: Blue resistance bars differ among the offspring. People choose the most resistant young trees. Then they cross those back to American chestnuts and test again. That is artificial selection. People choose which trees reproduce, instead of letting the environment alone decide.

scenes.tts: The goal is not simply more differences. It is inherited resistance strong enough to help trees survive, make seeds, and grow a next generation. Other traits still matter, but they cannot replace resistance to this fungus.
scenes.caption: The goal is not simply more differences. It is inherited resistance strong enough to help trees survive, make seeds, and grow a next generation. Other traits still matter, but they cannot replace resistance to this fungus.
scenes.visual: Return the chosen seedlings to the forest opening. Their BLUE bars stay visible as RED cankers approach. Some remain GREEN, produce YELLOW seeds, and their seedlings rise toward the canopy. Briefly show varied leaf shapes beside them; the shapes slide away while the blue resistance bars remain. A generation arrow completes from parents to seedlings.
scenes.narration: The goal is not simply more differences. It is inherited resistance strong enough to help trees survive, make seeds, and grow a next generation. Other traits still matter, but they cannot replace resistance to this fungus.

scenes.tts: Crossing does not promise recovery. Breeders need repeated tests across many families and sites. These tests ask how well young trees survive and resist blight.
scenes.caption: Crossing does not promise recovery. Breeders need repeated tests across many families and sites. These tests ask how well young trees survive and resist blight.
scenes.visual: Duplicate the same seedling family into three schematic forest panels with different soil and light backgrounds. Its BLUE bars stay identical, but RED canker growth and green survival differ by panel. Label each panel 'schematic site'. Replace a single crown icon over one family with several test clipboards spread across families. Never label any family best or proven.
scenes.narration: Crossing does not promise recovery. Breeders need repeated tests across many families and sites. These tests ask how well young trees survive and resist blight.

scenes.tts: Some scientists have also tried adding one gene from wheat. In tests, it helped American chestnuts resist blight. That work is still being checked. Both paths ask one question. Will enough trees survive, reproduce, and keep reproducing?
scenes.caption: Some scientists have also tried adding one gene from wheat. In tests, it helped American chestnuts resist blight. That work is still being checked. Both paths ask one question. Will enough trees survive, reproduce, and keep reproducing?
scenes.visual: Do not draw a molecule. Show one labeled block 'wheat gene' with a small tag 'still being checked' moving into a plain chestnut cell icon, then transform that icon into a young tree with a BLUE resistance bar. Place it beside the breeding path, not above it. Both paths feed into the same forest test and the same yellow generation arrow. End with the population question above both paths.
scenes.narration: Some scientists have also tried adding one gene from wheat. In tests, it helped American chestnuts resist blight. That work is still being checked. Both paths ask one question. Will enough trees survive, reproduce, and keep reproducing?

scenes.tts: Return to the underground root. A sprout alone keeps the past alive. Seed-making trees can begin the future. For this forest, recovery means living through blight and producing the next generation.
scenes.caption: Return to the underground root. A sprout alone keeps the past alive. Seed-making trees can begin the future. For this forest, recovery means living through blight and producing the next generation.
scenes.visual: Slide back to the original GREEN root. On the left, its lone sprout loops through a RED canker with no seeds. On the right, two trees with visible BLUE bars survive and fill part of the empty canopy. Pollen drifts between them before YELLOW seeds fall and become seedlings. Transform the stopped generation arrow into a completed arrow on the right.
scenes.narration: Return to the underground root. A sprout alone keeps the past alive. Seed-making trees can begin the future. For this forest, recovery means living through blight and producing the next generation.

scenes.tts: That is why the chestnut can remain alive yet fail to recover. The rule for this film is narrower: survival requires survivors to reproduce, not merely remain alive.
scenes.caption: That is why the chestnut can remain alive yet fail to recover. The rule for this film is narrower: survival requires survivors to reproduce, not merely remain alive.
scenes.visual: Dim the looping sprout on the left but keep it GREEN. Brighten the two seed-making trees and yellow seedlings on the right. Move the complete generation arrow to the center and write the film rule above it. Keep both cases visible so 'alive' is not confused with 'extinct'.
scenes.narration: That is why the chestnut can remain alive yet fail to recover. The rule for this film is narrower: survival requires survivors to reproduce, not merely remain alive.

scenes.visual: Dim the forest while the seed-making trees and seedlings sway slowly. Show one centered line only in large white text: 'Survival requires survivors to reproduce, not merely remain alive.'
